after: ## Issues at global, national and local level
alt: Four rings from personal to global for language change: a grandparent and grandchild who no longer share a first language; a local language class closing; national choices about which languages schools teach; and smaller languages declining globally as a few languages spread.
caption: One issue, such as language decline, can be traced from the global level down to a single family.

after: ## Perspectives: who sees the change differently and why
alt: Six groups around a market closure: long-standing residents, younger residents, traders, the local council, newcomers and heritage organisations, each with their view. Below, three drivers of perspectives: values, interests and experience.
caption: Cultural change has winners and losers, so perspectives on one change differ sharply.

after: ## Perspectives: who sees the change differently and why
alt: An older resident says the tea house closing means neighbours stop knowing each other. Four tagged steps analyse it: knowledge of the claim, application to a value and experience, analysis of the link between place and social ties, and evaluation that it is plausible but unsupported.
caption: Move from what is said, to why, to how the reasoning works, to how well it is supported.

alt: Five common causes of cultural change (globalised media, movement of people, economic change, government policy, tourism) above a four-step chain: rents rise, long-standing families move out, fewer children attend the local language class, and the class closes. A list of separate points is contrasted with a linked chain.
caption: Linking each cause to the next consequence is what turns a list into analysis.

alt: In a fictional village, the bus cut (dashed arrow, speeds it up) and the pull of jobs in town (solid arrow) both lead young people to move to town. Fewer people then take part in the harvest festival, and older residents carry it alone. The evaluation notes the bus cut may speed up a change rather than create it.
caption: Ask whether a cause creates a change or only speeds it up.

alt: An invented source claims 80% of teenagers prefer global pop, so local music has no future. Four checks fail: unknown producer, unknown method and sample, a conclusion that does not follow, and emotive language. Four reasoning flaws are listed: appeal to tradition, appeal to novelty, false dilemma and generalisation.
caption: The conclusion goes far beyond what a preference survey can show.

after: ## Courses of action and their effects
alt: Five types of action (record, teach, share spaces, fund and protect, adapt) above an assessment of free dialect classes: the action targets the lack of chances to learn; if it works, children hear the dialect at home; the risk is that it only records the dialect; the judgement is that it works better combined with local signs and events.
caption: An action is judged by whether it tackles the cause and lasts once enthusiasm fades.
